extracted.intended_audience: general public, consumers, regulators, and companies involved in rulemaking or public-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether public comments submitted to rulemaking or legislative proceedings are genuine, voluntary, and traceable to real individuals (not fabricated, impersonated, or generated deceptively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consumer identities with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must not use the identities of consumers without their knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OAG found the fake comments "used the identities of millions of consumers, including thousands of New Yorkers, without their knowledge or consent." Anti-pattern: submitting comments that impersonate people who did not agree to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No impersonation of Americans in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments should not impersonate Americans or otherwise present false authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General James called out companies for "impersonating Americans without their knowledge or consent." Example of misconduct: mass-submitting comments that attribute views to real people who did not provide them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on fabricated responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses submitted as public comments must be genuine and not fabricated by vendors or intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead generators "simply fabricated consumers’ responses." Specific instances: LCX and Lead ID each fabricated responses for 1.5 million consumers; Ifficient supplied more than 840,000 fake responses. Anti-pattern: hiring lead generators who invent commenter data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic digital signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital signatures and petition signatures must be generated by the genuine signatories, not produced fraudulently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigation found more than 3.5 million fake digital signatures for letters and petitions. Fraudulent generation of signatures undermines the integrity of correspondence to legislators and officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about who generated or funded comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns that generate large numbers of comments should disclose who funded or organized the comment collection and whether commercial vendors were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAG reports that "the nation’s largest broadband companies funded a secret campaign" and engaged commercial lead generators; lack of disclosure provided "cover" for policy outcomes. Guidance: failure to disclose funding/organizers is an abusive practice that can obscure industry influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful and non-deceptive solicitation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods used to solicit consumer participation (ads, prizes, sweepstakes, etc.) must not be followed by deceptive practices that substitute fabricated responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead generators used "advertisements and prizes, like gift cards and sweepstakes entries, to encourage consumers to join the campaign," yet many firms then fabricated responses instead of enrolling real consumers. Anti-pattern: offering inducements while producing fake entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding contamination across proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment-generation practices must not recycle or contaminate other governmental proceedings by using the same fabricated or misattributed responses across multiple agencies or campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OAG found that fraud "infected other government proceedings as well," generating fake comments for EPA, BOEM, Congress, and other federal and state officials. Example: LCX fabricated responses across four advocacy campaigns; Lead ID fabricated in multiple campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability through enforcement and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities that supply fake comments, impersonate individuals, or otherwise engage in fraudulent comment-generation are subject to penalties, disgorgement, and civil enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreements required the companies and their principals to pay specified penalties and disgorgement (e.g., LCX paying $400,000 to New York and $100,000 to San Diego; Lead ID $30,000 to New York; Ifficient $63,750 to New York and $21,250 to Colorado). Enforcement cooperation across jurisdictions (state AGs, district attorneys) is an available remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving public-comment opportunities as genuine input
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comment opportunities should remain a chance for Americans to give their input on government policies and must not be co-opted by manipulative commercial practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General James emphasized: "Public comment opportunities are a chance for Americans to give their input on important government policies, and these companies abused that for their own selfish purposes." Guidance implies that legitimate comment campaigns should reflect actual public views rather than manufactured mass submissions.
